To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
arsenite induces a copper accumulation in the kidney of rats which is parallel to arsenic accumulation in the kidney, liver, and red blood cells.
arsenite induces a copper accumulation in the kidney cortex which is synchroneous with the accumulation of arsenic.
arsenic and the essential trace element copper accumulate in the rat kidney in a synchronous manner and at a ratio of 1:3.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the time course of the arsenite-induced renal copper accumulation in rats, and with the mechanisms involved.
the mechanisms of the arsenite-induced renal copper accumulation.
the mechanisms of arsenic-induced renal copper accumulation in rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the arsenic-induced renal copper accumulation is not a toxic effect of arsenic but a functional relationship between both metals with respect to renal retention.
the renal copper accumulation after arsenite administration is not due to a general toxic effect on the kidney.
arsenic and renal copper accumulation are interrelated phenomena.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the accumulation of both arsenic (toxic) and copper (essential) is organ-specific and time dependent.
arsenic and arsenic compounds are capable of altering the renal copper homeostasis in the rat.
arsenic induces a renal copper accumulation in the rat, which is not caused by an interference with biliary or hepatic copper transport.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accumulation of arsenic in the kidney is paralleled by a similar accumulation of copper, and that both metals seem to have a functional relationship with regard to their renal retention.
the renal copper accumulation in arsenite-treated rats was a slow process that took place over the entire 12 d of treatment.
arsenic exposure can lead to an accumulation and retention of copper in the renal cortex, and that this accumulation is not a transient phenomenon but rather persists after termination of exposure.
